glance.why: Shanghai is the only Chinese city that was largely built by outsiders and then took itself back. The result is a place with no imperial axis and no single centre, where a 1920s banking facade faces a 632-metre tower across a muddy river, and the best afternoon you can have is aimless walking under plane trees in the old French Concession. It is China's most comfortable city for a first-time visitor and its least representative.
dontMiss: The Bund at dusk, then again at 7am when it is empty
Aimless walking in the former French Concession
Yu Garden early, before the bazaar fills
The skyline from the Pudong side, or from a Bund rooftop
One water town or a Suzhou day trip

history.story: Shanghai spent most of Chinese history as an unremarkable cotton and fishing town. Everything that makes it interesting happened in the last 180 years, starting with a war fought over the right to sell opium, and the city has been catching up with, and then overtaking, that origin ever since.
history.origins: A walled market town at the mouth of the Yangtze, useful for coastal shipping and cotton, entirely overshadowed by Suzhou and Hangzhou.

periods.name: Treaty port, 1842-1943
periods.text: The Treaty of Nanking opened Shanghai to foreign trade and created the International Settlement and the French Concession, foreign-run enclaves with their own police and courts. Money, opium, banking and printing poured in.

periods.name: The 1920s and 30s
periods.text: The Paris of the East and the whore of the Orient, depending on who was writing. Jazz clubs, gangsters, Chinese modernist literature, the founding of the Communist Party in a Concession shikumen house, and the largest refugee community of European Jews in Asia.

periods.name: War and revolution, 1937-1949
periods.text: Japanese occupation, then the Communist victory. Capital, industry and much of the elite left for Hong Kong and Taiwan.

periods.name: Socialist decades, 1949-1990
periods.text: Shanghai became an industrial workhorse taxed to fund the rest of the country. The Bund buildings became government offices; Pudong was farmland and warehouses.

periods.name: Reform, 1990-
periods.text: Deng Xiaoping's decision to develop Pudong turned a floodplain into the skyline you photograph, in one generation.

history.modern: Shanghai now runs on finance, shipping, design and consumption. It is China's wealthiest large city and the one most legible to a foreigner, which is precisely why some Chinese visitors find it inauthentic. The trade-off for the visitor is real: everything is easy, and you will learn less about China than you would in Xi'an or Chengdu.
history.whyItMatters: The city's whole aesthetic is negotiation between imported and local. Shikumen houses are British terraces with Chinese courtyard gates. The food is Jiangnan sweetness plus everything that arrived by ship. The art scene lives in repurposed industry because industry is what the socialist decades left behind.
visible: The Bund is a catalogue of 1920s banking architecture, read left to right as you walk north.
Shikumen lane houses in the Concession show the hybrid at domestic scale; Xintiandi is the restored version, Tianzifang the messier one.
Wukang Mansion, the flatiron block on Huaihai Road, is the single most photographed piece of that era.
The Jewish Refugees Museum in Hongkou marks where 20,000 people sheltered from the Holocaust.
Power Station of Art and M50 are socialist industry turned into culture.

historic.name: The Bund
historic.why: A mile of 1920s granite facing the towers. Walk it at dusk for the lights and again at dawn for the tai chi and the emptiness.

historic.name: Yu Garden
historic.why: A Ming scholar's garden of rockeries, dragon walls and zigzag bridges. Go at opening; the surrounding bazaar is a scrum by ten.

historic.name: Shikumen Open House Museum
historic.why: A restored lane house furnished as it was in the 1930s. The best single explanation of how Shanghai actually lived.

historic.name: Jewish Refugees Museum
historic.why: The Ohel Moishe synagogue and the story of the Shanghai ghetto. Small, sober, worth the trip.

historic.name: Longhua Temple
historic.why: The city's oldest temple with a wooden pagoda dating to the tenth century. Working, incense-thick, largely local.

arts.name: Shanghai Museum
arts.why: Free and genuinely world-class. The bronze and ceramic galleries are the reason; skip the rest if pressed. A second, larger branch has opened in Pudong.

arts.name: Power Station of Art
arts.why: A former power plant, China's first state-run contemporary art museum. Ambitious, uneven, always interesting.

arts.name: West Bund museum mile
arts.why: Long Museum, Yuz Museum and the Centre Pompidou outpost strung along the riverside. A half day if the shows are good.

arts.name: M50
arts.why: Suzhou Creek warehouses full of working studios and small galleries. Rougher and more real than West Bund.

arts.name: Propaganda Poster Art Centre
arts.why: In the basement of an apartment block, a private collection of 1950s-70s posters. Strange, excellent, tiny.

nature.name: Fuxing Park
nature.why: French-laid-out park where retirees dance, play cards and sing. Best before 9am.

nature.name: Century Park
nature.why: The big green one, good for cycling.

nature.name: Suzhou Creek walkway
nature.why: A restored riverside walk past converted warehouses; the quieter alternative to the Bund.

nature.name: Shanghai Botanical Garden or Chenshan

shopping.why: Independent design, concept stores, the best browsing in the city.

shopping.name: Nanjing Road
shopping.why: The famous pedestrian shopping street. Crowded and mostly chains; walk it once for the neon.

shopping.name: Tianzifang
shopping.why: Craft and souvenir shops in lane houses. Touristy but pleasant early.

shopping.name: Dongtai Road antiques (much reduced) and Yuyuan bazaar
shopping.why: Chops, fans, tea things and reproductions. Bargain.

shopping.name: Zhangyuan
shopping.why: Restored shikumen block turned into luxury retail. Architecturally interesting even if you buy nothing.

nightlife.why: You pay for the view once. Bar Rouge, Vue and the Peninsula terrace all deliver it.

nightlife.name: Speakeasy cocktail bars

nightlife.name: Live music at Yuyintang

food.identity: Shanghainese cooking belongs to the Jiangnan tradition: sweeter, oilier and more delicate than northern food, built on river fish, freshwater shrimp, soy and sugar rather than chilli. Locals call the signature technique nong you chi jiang, heavy oil and red sauce. Layered on top is everything that arrived by port, so the city also has China's best coffee, its most serious bar scene and long-established Cantonese, Japanese and Western cooking.

mustTry.what: Thin-skinned pork dumplings with jellied stock inside that melts into soup when steamed.
mustTry.why: Invented in Nanxiang on the city's edge, and the technical benchmark for dumpling-making.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: Nip the side, drink the soup, then eat. Vinegar with ginger shreds, never soy.

mustTry.what: Thicker-skinned pork buns pan-fried until the base is crisp, sesame and scallion on top.
mustTry.why: The breakfast counterpart to xiaolongbao and, for many locals, the better dumpling.
mustTry.flavour: Crunchy bottom, soft top, soup inside.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: From a shop window, standing, two or four at a time.

mustTry.what: Pork belly braised in soy, sugar and rice wine until glossy and collapsing.
mustTry.why: The archetypal red-cooked dish and the clearest expression of the local sweet-savoury balance.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: With plain rice, as part of a shared table.

mustTry.what: Live freshwater shrimp or raw crab cured in strong rice wine.
mustTry.why: A genuinely local delicacy that most visitors never try.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: As a cold starter. Be aware it is raw.

mustTry.what: Small freshwater crab steamed whole, eaten with vinegar and ginger. Autumn only.
mustTry.why: A seasonal obsession that shuts down conversation in October and November.
mustTry.flavour: Sweet roe, delicate meat, a great deal of work.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: With yellow wine, slowly, at a table of people who will show you how.
mustTry.importance: Essential if you visit in autumn

mustTry.what: Noodles tossed in scallion oil with dried shrimp and soy.
mustTry.why: Three ingredients, no protein, and one of the great cheap bowls anywhere.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: For lunch, alone, in five minutes.

mustTry.what: Spicy crayfish, seasonal, eaten with gloves.
mustTry.why: Summer street food; more Hunan than Shanghai in origin but adopted wholeheartedly.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: Outdoors in summer, messily, in groups.

mustTry.dish: Sheng jian and da bing you tiao breakfast
mustTry.what: Fried dough sticks, rice rolls, soy milk and pancakes from a morning shop.
mustTry.why: The four heavenly kings of Shanghai breakfast, still eaten daily.

iconic.name: Jia Jia Tang Bao
iconic.desc: Cramped, functional, and the soup dumpling locals name first. Sells out.

iconic.name: Old Jesse (Lao Ji Shi)
iconic.desc: Tiny, legendary, ferociously popular. Home-style cooking taken seriously.
iconic.whyGo: The best-known expression of the local cuisine.

iconic.name: Fairmont Peace Hotel jazz bar
iconic.desc: 1929 lobby bar with the old jazz band still playing.
iconic.whyGo: The clearest surviving piece of 1930s Shanghai.

bestFood.name: Fu He Hui
bestFood.desc: Buddhist-influenced vegetarian tasting menus, meditative rooms.
bestFood.whyGo: One of the best restaurants in China, meat or not.

bestFood.name: Ultraviolet
bestFood.desc: Ten seats, one table, multi-sensory. You are collected from a meeting point.
bestFood.whyGo: If you want the most-discussed dining experience in Asia.

bestFood.name: Fu 1088
bestFood.desc: Private rooms in a 1930s villa, refined versions of local classics.
bestFood.whyGo: Shanghainese food in the setting it deserves.

bestValue.name: Yang's Fry Dumpling
bestValue.desc: A chain, still excellent, still cheap.
bestValue.whyGo: The best five-minute meal in the city.

bestValue.name: Nanxiang Steamed Bun Restaurant
bestValue.desc: The famous one by the garden. Tourist-heavy, but the upstairs rooms are calmer and good.

bestValue.name: Neighbourhood noodle shops in the Concession

special.name: Mr & Mrs Bund

special.whyGo: A special dinner with the view.

special.name: Canton Table or a hotel Cantonese room

casual.desc: Morning-only shops selling the four heavenly kings.

cafes.name: Metal Hands, Manner, Seesaw and a hundred others
cafes.desc: Shanghai has more coffee shops than any city on earth and the standard is high.
cafes.whyGo: Fuel for a walking day, and a genuine local obsession.

cafes.name: Sunflour or Baker & Spice
cafes.desc: Proper bread and pastry, a legacy of the concession years.

cafes.name: Huxinting Teahouse
cafes.desc: The zigzag-bridge teahouse in the middle of the bazaar pond.

experiences.name: Morning in Fuxing Park
experiences.what: Ballroom dancing, choirs, cards, tai chi, all before 9am.
experiences.why: The friendliest hour in the city and completely free.

experiences.name: Huangpu River ferry
experiences.what: The public commuter ferry between Puxi and Pudong for a couple of yuan.
experiences.why: The same view as the cruise, at one percent of the price.

experiences.name: A cocktail bar crawl in the Concession
experiences.what: Three or four of the small bars around Anfu and Yongkang.
experiences.why: Shanghai's bartending is genuinely world class.

experiences.name: Shikumen lane wandering
experiences.what: Push into the residential lanes off Anfu or Wukang and see laundry, mahjong and daily life.
experiences.why: The city at domestic scale, thirty seconds from the boutiques.

experiences.name: Tailoring at the fabric market
experiences.what: South Bund Fabric Market: pick cloth, get measured, collect in a few days.

timeGuidance.three: Day 1 the Bund, Yu Garden and Shanghai Museum. Day 2 the Concession on foot, all day, with a museum and a rooftop. Day 3 a water town or Suzhou.
timeGuidance.fivePlus: Add West Bund or Power Station of Art, Hongkou, a fabric-market fitting, a bar night, and a second unhurried Concession afternoon.

dayTrips.name: Suzhou
dayTrips.why: Classical scholar gardens, canals and silk. The single best day trip in eastern China.
dayTrips.logistics: Trains every few minutes from Hongqiao. Book the Humble Administrator's Garden ahead.

dayTrips.name: Hangzhou
dayTrips.why: West Lake, tea villages and temples. Better as an overnight than a day trip.
dayTrips.suits: Anyone with a spare day and a taste for landscape.

dayTrips.name: Zhujiajiao
dayTrips.why: The closest canal town. Pretty, restored and busy at weekends.
dayTrips.logistics: Metro all the way; go on a weekday morning.
dayTrips.verdict: Worth it if you cannot reach Suzhou

dayTrips.name: Wuzhen or Xitang
dayTrips.why: Larger, better-preserved water towns; Wuzhen's east gate is lovely in the evening.
dayTrips.verdict: Worth it if you stay overnight

dayTrips.name: Nanjing
dayTrips.why: Ming walls, the tomb, and the Nanjing Massacre Memorial. Historically heavy, rewarding.
dayTrips.suits: Anyone interested in modern Chinese history.
dayTrips.verdict: Only if you have extra time

practical.gettingAround: The metro is excellent, cheap and signed in English; lines 2 and 10 cover most of what you want. Set up a transit code in Alipay before you arrive. Didi for taxis. The Concession is best walked, and bike-share works well on flat ground. The Maglev from Pudong airport is fun for eight minutes but drops you at Longyang Road, which is inconvenient unless you are heading east.
practical.whenToGo: October and November are the best: dry, mild, and hairy crab season. Late March to May is good, with magnolia and plane trees coming into leaf. Summer is hot, humid and typhoon-prone. Winter is grey, damp and colder than the latitude suggests because buildings are poorly heated. Avoid the first week of October.

howLong.one: The Bund, Yu Garden and a Concession walk. Rushed but coherent.
howLong.twoThree: Add the Shanghai Museum, a rooftop, and a proper Shanghainese dinner. This is the sweet spot.
howLong.fourFive: Add a water town or Suzhou, a contemporary art half day, and Hongkou.
howLong.week: Use it as a base for Suzhou, Hangzhou and a water town overnight.

culture: Bring your passport; it is needed for museums, rail and hotels.
Payment is by phone. Set up Alipay or WeChat Pay with a foreign card before arrival.
A VPN installed before you land is necessary for most non-Chinese services.
Shanghainese is a distinct language, not a dialect of Mandarin, and older residents may prefer it.
Restaurants turn tables quickly at lunch; lingering is a dinner and cafe activity.
Book the big-name restaurants well ahead; the good small ones do not take bookings at all.

whatIdDo.plan: Yu Garden at opening, then walk to the Bund and along it. Shanghai Museum after lunch. Sunset from a Bund rooftop, dinner at Jia Jia Tang Bao or a Concession noodle shop.

Fuxing Park before nine, then the entire day walking the Concession: Wukang Mansion, Anfu Road, the Propaganda Poster Centre, coffee twice. Cocktails, then dinner at Fu 1088 or Old Jesse if you booked.
High-speed rail to Suzhou at eight. Humble Administrator's Garden, the Master of the Nets, lunch, a canal walk, back by seven.
Power Station of Art or the West Bund museums, riverside cycling, Longhua Temple. Evening ferry across the river and a last look at the skyline.

musts: The Bund at dusk and dawn
